prompt: Assume an illustrative rate of ten billion unsalted SHA-256 candidates per second. Roughly how long to exhaust all eight-character passwords from the 94 non-space printable ASCII characters (8 copies of 94 multiplied together, about 6.1 × 10^15 possibilities)?

options.explanation: Ten billion guesses a second into about 6.1 thousand million million possibilities gives 610,000 seconds, not 600 seconds. Check the exponent subtraction: the power becomes five.

Correct under the assumed rate: about 610,000 seconds, or seven days. Each unsalted candidate digest can be checked against all hashes using that scheme; this search only covers the stipulated password space.
That is the figure if each guess cost ten thousand times more (a slow hash). Fast SHA-256 doesn't add that cost.

options.text: Longer than the age of the universe
options.explanation: At the assumed rate and search space, the calculation gives about seven days. No general hardware claim or comparison with every 128-bit system is needed.

workedExample:
Divide the number of possible passwords by the guess rate, then convert seconds to days:

```formula
T = S / G
T = 6.1 × 10^15 / (10^10 per s)
T = 6.1 × 10^5 s
T = (6.1 × 10^5 / 86400) days
T ≈ 7.1 days
where
T: the worst-case time to try every password once
S: the search space: 94^8 ≈ 6.1 × 10^15 passwords
G: the assumed guess rate, 10^10 per second
s: seconds
86400: seconds in a day (24 × 60 × 60)
days: the unit of the final answer
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: ten billion guesses a second exhausts the whole space in about a week.
```

The large numerator and rate use powers of ten; dividing them subtracts their exponents. The *average* time is half the worst case, about 3.5 days. This is why fast hashes are unsuitable for passwords: the defender needs each guess to be expensive, which is what Argon2id, scrypt and bcrypt provide.
